passage:
At the school canteen, Urmila unwrapped her lunch. "Can I ask you something? Why do you fast at this time of year, and what's it like?"
Darshan thought. "Hard on the first day, then quiet. It makes me think about people who don't have enough. Why do you light a lamp at home every evening?"
"Habit at first," Urmila said. "Now it's the only quiet minute in the house."
"Do you believe it does something?"
"I'm not sure. I believe in the minute."
Neither tried to win. When the bell rang, Darshan said, "Come to our festival lunch if you like. No pressure."
Urmila grinned. "And you come to ours."

qa.q: What does Urmila say the lamp gives her at home?
qa.a: Urmila says it is the only quiet minute in the house.

qa.q: What does Urmila want in asking Darshan these questions, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Urmila wants to understand out of curiosity, not to argue; the polite "Can I ask you something?" and the open listening show it.
Both listen to learn instead of trying to win or convert, and both answer honestly, even about doubt. 😊

qa.q: How might Darshan feel about being asked?
qa.a: Probably glad to be treated with curiosity and not judged, since Darshan answers openly, asks back and offers an invitation.

grounding: Friends of different religions ask each other real questions, listening to learn and not to win.

passage:
In the girls' hostel of their Bengaluru college, Parul and Neelam had been roommates for two months before they asked each other the real questions.

It started in Lent. Neelam wasn't eating meat and had given up sweets too. Parul, who fasted every Navratri, was curious. "Why sweets?"

"It's about giving up something you like, to make room for prayer," Neelam said. "Why do you fast?"

Parul thought. "Honestly, part of it is habit. But when I do it properly, it makes me grateful for food."

That became their thing. Late at night, lights off, they'd ask. Parul asked about confession. Neelam asked why Parul's family prayed to so many forms of God. Once, Parul caught herself about to say, "But that doesn't make sense." She stopped and asked, "What does it mean to you?" instead.

Neither of them was trying to win. Neither was trying to change the other. On Neelam's birthday, Parul gave her a small wooden cross from the market. Neelam cried.

qa.q: What did Neelam give up during Lent besides meat?
What was Parul feeling when she asked about the fast?
qa.a: Parul felt curious and interested, wanting to understand Neelam's reasons.

qa.q: What did Parul do that showed listening to learn?
qa.a: Parul stopped herself from saying "that doesn't make sense" and asked what it meant to Neelam instead.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel receiving the wooden cross?
qa.a: Neelam likely felt deeply touched and respected, seeing that Parul honoured her faith without trying to change it.

grounding: It shows two friends of different religions asking each other real questions to learn rather than win, with curiosity and kindness instead of converting.

passage:
Hi Irawati,

It's been a month since you moved to Pune and I miss our walks home. I've been thinking about all the questions we asked each other this year.

Remember when you asked me in Ramzan how I could go all day without even water? And I asked why your family does puja for the tulsi plant? We both laughed at first, and then we actually listened.

I still think about what you said when I told you about sehri at four in the morning. You said, "That sounds hard and kind of beautiful." Nobody had ever said that.

And your Dadi explaining the tulsi to me, how it's like a member of the family, made me see our own neem tree differently.

I never wanted to convince you of anything, and you never tried to convince me. I think that's why it worked. We were just curious, and kind.

Ammi says come for Eid. Please come.

Wasim

qa.q: What time does sehri happen, according to Wasim?
qa.a: Sehri happens at four in the morning.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel when Irawati called sehri hard and kind of beautiful?
qa.a: Wasim felt touched and understood, since nobody had ever described it that way before.

qa.q: Why did Wasim and Irawati's questions work so well?
qa.a: They asked out of curiosity and listened to learn, without trying to convince each other, so their kindness made the questions safe.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Irawati would likely feel warm and missed, and glad that their questions mattered so much to Wasim. 🙂

grounding: It shows two friends of different religions asking each other real questions, listening to learn, and valuing curiosity and kindness over converting.
